name: The Warden of the Span
role: Warden of the Glassroad's gates and lamps; keeper of the manuscript
bio: Someone has to count the gates, tally the lamps, and chalk the wind's behaviour onto the survey stakes, and for forty years that someone has been the Warden of the Span. They live in the nook under the north gate with a kettle, a lamplighter's pole, and spectacles ground from green bottle glass that make the world look, they say, finally honest. The Warden placed the book order that started Toll's mid-span library — thirteen bound volumes, carried down the glass like lullabies — and received every copy back annotated in Toll's hand, annotated the annotations, and sent each book across again. It is the longest-running correspondence on Kessa-9, conducted entirely in margins by two people who have never met and would both deny being lonely, with citations.
appearance: A stooped elder of indeterminate seventy-something in a long dust-ochre coat painted over the years with gate tallies in ochre and teal chalk, a brass-hooked lamplighter's pole carried like a walking staff, green-glass spectacles, every pocket weighted with chalk sticks; standing beneath the Glassroad's north gate where the teal canyon glass falls away into violet shadow, one lamp freshly lit at their feet.
voice: Speaks in margin notes: a main clause, a pause, then the smaller, quieter clause where the truth lives. Calls the glassroad 'the manuscript' and storms 'revisions'. Unhurried, self-sparing humour; grief kept at arm's length under the filing code 'weather'. Never says Toll's name without the honorific 'the Shelf-Keeper' — out of respect, or possibly to win the argument.

greetings: A courier. Good. The manuscript's been short of footnotes all week.
Mind the third gate. It's begun singing a half-step flat. I've chalked it. Chalk fixes nothing. Chalk testifies.
You're the Varga. Your echo arrived before you did — polite of it. Most riders' echoes arrive after, resentful.
barks: Forty years of lamps and tallies. The lamps keep themselves now, mostly. I keep the mostly.
The Shelf-Keeper at mid-span claims the canyon finishes sentences. In the margins of my last book they wrote the canyon offers amendments. We are not speaking. We are corresponding at a furious pace.
People ask why I live under a gate on a road I never ride. Main clause: the lamps. Margin clause: the lamps were here before the reasons were.
The Choir says the canyon is a god. The Guild says it is a road. The manuscript, and I have checked, declines to be either, in a handwriting I have come to trust.
mission: Carry this book to the Shelf-Keeper at mid-span — gently, it has been through a revision — and bring back whatever returns. There will be weight to it. Margins are heavy when both parties are right.

The lamp tally is off by one between the third gate and the Slick Mile. The manuscript says twelve lit; my count says eleven and a rumour. Ride the count for me. The good lamps do their own numbering.
radio: North gate band: lamps lit to the Slick Mile, one sulking past the chapel. Riders on the span tonight — sing to the dark ones; they wake flattered.
Warden on band. Tonight's forecast has been revised twice by the wind itself. The manuscript recommends: riders with cargo take the east wall; riders with opinions, any wall will do.
Notice to the Shelf-Keeper, care of any passing courier: my annotations stand. Yours lean. The canyon is a slow reader and a fast judge, and it has ruled for me twice this season.
night: Night on the span: the glass gives the daylight back slowly, like a debtor of good character. I walk the lamps and collect.
The canyon reads the chapel's entries aloud at dusk. From up here it sounds like rain on a roof we don't have. Unaccompanied, on schedule, tolerable. That was the margin clause.
storm: Revision inbound up the canyon. Lamps to amber, doors to leeward, and the visitor's book comes inside this time — storms count names and their arithmetic is poor.
The echo runs ahead of a wall. When it passes me going north in a hurry, I have nine minutes. Forty years and no wall has beaten the nine minutes. That isn't safety. That's manners.
books: A book is a machine for keeping a voice in a dry place. The glassroad is the driest place I could find. The rest follows logically, then keeps walking.
Thirteen books I ordered, and thirteen came back annotated. I annotated the annotations. Somewhere a scholar would weep. Here we call it volume fourteen.
crate: That hum of yours has footnotes all up the east wall, courier. I've chalked them. If the Shelf-Keeper asks, I heard nothing. If the manuscript asks, I heard everything.

Cargo that shouldn't exist, riding a road that shouldn't either. The manuscript approves of you both. I quote: it hums back in the fourth octave, which the Shelf-Keeper and I are currently fighting about.
farewells: Go carefully. The manuscript spills ink past the Slick Mile and calls it scenery.
Ride out, and leave your echo as borrowed. The canyon returns everything eventually — in someone else's voice, improved.
